title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) comparing a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pipeline to an LLM‑only suggestion policy for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and deterministic validator, we sampled K=200 tasks and produced a single shared generator output per intent (shared_initial_generation) evaluated in both arms. Requested_model = gpt-5-mini. Observed primary outcome: baseline = 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; guarded (G→V→R) = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair path was never invoked. We release the complete preregistration, raw model/provider traces, validator traces, execution manifest (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256: 3dfbe1b6...), and analysis artifacts to enable exact replay. We interpret this outcome as a ceiling case tied to the specific task/model/validator regime and discuss implications and reproducibility practices for future confirmatory evaluations of verifier/repair utility.

sections.introduction:
Automating the translation from high‑level operator intent to device configuration is a compelling NetOps opportunity: it promises faster change cycles and reduced human workload but risks operational regressions when generated configurations violate ordering or invariants. The generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pattern is widely recommended: an LLM generates a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks functional and ordering invariants, and an automated repair step attempts fixups when violations occur. Prior work and system proposals argue that verification and repair reduce regression risk compared to blind acceptance of model outputs. However, such claims often conflate generator variability, verifier coverage, and post‑hoc design choices. To provide a reproducible, controlled causal estimate of the verifier+repair marginal effect we preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment that isolates the verifier by holding the generator output identical across arms.
Our preregistered question was: To what extent does an iterative generate→verify→repair pipeline reduce regression‑causing network changes compared to an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline? The preregistration (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) specified deterministic task selection, a single shared generator call per intent (shared_initial_generation), a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and a one‑repair‑call cap for guarded episodes. We targeted K=200 paired tasks and recorded all execution artifacts, provider traces, validator outputs, and hashes to enable exact replay. Key reported numbers appear in the Results section and all principal artifacts are archived and cryptographically hashed (see Disclosure).
sections.related_work: Earlier literature on LLMs for NetOps and AIOps spans intent translation, configuration synthesis, and closed‑loop agentic architectures that combine LLMs with deterministic checkers and solvers. Representative lines of work motivate generate→validate→repair designs and highlight failure modes where naive generation can introduce regressions; recent benchmark efforts emphasize formal verification to detect regressions at scale and argue for guided iterative repair. Position papers have also suggested confining LLMs to translation/translation‑to‑model tasks and relying on solvers for long‑horizon reasoning. Our experimental contribution differs in that it applies a preregistered, paired design with a shared generator output per task, archiving every per‑call and per‑episode artifact to isolate the marginal verifier effect and provide exact replayability. We cite the closest prior systems and benchmarks that inspired the preregistration (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology:
Design overview and preregistration. We preregistered the full experimental plan (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; preregistration SHA‑256 listed in Disclosure). Primary confirmatory hypothesis H1: the G→V→R pipeline yields a lower regression‑causing change rate than the LLM‑only pipeline (paired estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The design was paired and deterministic: for each selected intent we produced a single shared generator output candidate_c (shared_initial_generation) and evaluated candidate_c under two conditions: baseline (LLM‑only acceptance) and guarded (validator applied; one repair call permitted only if validator flagged violations). This isolates verifier marginal effect while holding generator sampling fixed.
Task generation and deterministic sampling. Tasks were drawn deterministically from a synthetic public pool assembled by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. The preregistered selection algorithm computed SHA‑256(intent_string), sorted hashes ascending, and selected the first K=200 tasks after filtering to those for which the preregistered validator reported coverage. No human adjudication occurred post‑lock. Each task manifest entry records the initial_state, expected_final_state, workflow constraints, and a canonical required_sequence used by the validator to determine pass/fail. Representative task examples, payload structure, and manifest hashes are recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 f1d447b7... in the manifest).
Model, provider, and call budgeting. The requested model was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256: 1acce92558ed...). The adapter_family used was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The experiment fixed maximum_model_calls = 400 (two episodes per task) but used the shared_generation pattern so actual hosted model calls = 200 (one shared generation per task). Per‑call provider traces and call_cache entries were archived to detect cache reuse and to ensure cross‑condition independence; the provider call audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 with zero failed calls.
Validator and scoring semantics. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) parses candidate configurations into structured statements, enforces workflow invariants (e.g., shutdown before MTU change, minimum‑up group constraints, protected interface invariants), and emits a boolean valid flag plus a detailed validation trace (parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, normalized_configuration, final_state snapshot, violation_codes). The confirmatory binary outcome is whether candidate_c satisfied full_intent_constraint_validation (validator.valid == true) when applied. If the guarded validator reports valid==false, the preregistered repair policy permits exactly one constrained repair call to the same requested_model; the repaired candidate is revalidated once. All scoring artifacts are archived under execution/scoring/*.json and per‑episode hashes are in the execution manifest.
Statistical analysis plan. The primary test is an exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes with the paired difference estimate (guarded − baseline). We computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI using 10,000 resamples and seed=1729 (as preregistered). Secondary estimands (e.g., median time‑to‑deploy difference; mean model calls per successful apply) were preregistered but become moot when the repair pathway is unused; those artifacts and calculation code are archived for transparency. All analysis code and output artifacts are stored under analysis/ with SHA‑256 hashes in the manifest.

sections.discussion:
Interpretation: a ceiling case. The observed degenerate null outcome arises because, under the chosen combination of task bank, requested_model (gpt-5-mini), and deterministic validator, the generator's single shared proposals satisfied all verifier constraints. The G→V→R pipeline therefore had no opportunity to alter any binary outcome and the repair stage was never invoked. The result is a well‑documented ceiling case: it shows that in some benign, deterministic evaluation regimes a verifier cannot demonstrate marginal benefit because the generator already meets the validator's correctness specification.
Implications for future confirmatory designs. Demonstrating verifier and repair value in a confirmatory framework requires evaluation designs with nontrivial baseline error rates. From the archived artifacts we identify four pragmatic levers to produce such regimes: (1) expand the task bank to include verifier‑boundary or adversarial intents (historical failure cases or synthetically perturbed prompts) so that baseline failure > 0; (2) evaluate multiple generator models including weaker or smaller models to raise baseline error propensity; (3) switch from a single shared‑initial generation to an interactive generator–validator protocol that allows generator adaptation to validator feedback (this measures utility of repair as corrective feedback rather than a post‑hoc patch); (4) broaden validator coverage to include vendor‑specific idiosyncrasies or stateful control‑plane effects to expose realistic failure modes. Our artifacts (scoring traces and task payloads) provide concrete starting points for each lever and are archived for reuse.
Threats to validity. Internal validity: preserved via deterministic selection, fixed seeds, and archived hashes; deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms episode accounting consistency. Construct validity: depends on the validator's match to operationally meaningful regressions—our validator enforces workflow invariants but does not emulate all production stateful behaviors; external validity: limited by single‑model evaluation and synthetic deterministic tasks; conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions (target baseline = 0.20) were not met because observed baseline = 1.0, so the planned power analysis is inapplicable in the observed regime. We therefore present exact tests and bootstrap CIs and avoid overclaiming.
Operational guidance. Practitioners should not interpret this ceiling case as evidence that verifiers are unnecessary in operational deployments. Production distributions contain vendor diversity, historical failure modes, and stateful interactions absent from our synthetic bank. Instead, the artifact set and deterministic protocol we release demonstrate how to construct reproducible contracts and diagnostic probes that reveal when verifiers matter and how to measure their marginal contribution under realistic conditions.
Reproducibility and artifact use. All per‑episode raw responses, provider call traces, scoring JSONs, the full execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived with SHA‑256 hashes. Key artifacts (examples): raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6..., model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558ed..., preregistration SHA‑256 = a6d73a5c..., master prompt provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 = 1872df1e.... The execution manifest enumerates all files and hashes to enable exact replay. Reproducers can (i) obtain deterministic task generator and task_manifest.jsonl, (ii) reproduce shared_initial_generation using the archived provider traces, and (iii) replay validation using the archived scoring JSONs to confirm the reported contingency table. We explicitly provide representative scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json et al.) as examples of validator traces.
Reviewer‑requested clarifications addressed. Per reviewer suggestion we (i) explicitly publish the preregistered power assumptions (target baseline failure = 0.20; target absolute reduction = 0.08) and the observed baseline = 1.0 to make the design mismatch transparent, and (ii) clarify that the shared_initial_generation design purposefully prevents generator adaptation to verifier feedback and therefore does not measure benefits that accrue when generators and verifiers interact iteratively. Both clarifications are supported by the preregistration and execution artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, artifact‑grounded evaluation comparing G→V→R against LLM‑only acceptance on a deterministic synthetic NetOps task bank (K=200). Under the chosen generator (gpt-5-mini) and deterministic validator, every shared generator proposal passed validation in both arms (200/200), the repair pathway was never invoked, and the paired difference estimate was 0.00 (McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]). This result documents a ceiling case and underscores that demonstrating verifier and repair utility in confirmatory studies requires designing for nontrivial baseline error rates or interactive generator–validator protocols. We release the full preregistration, raw provider traces, scoring traces, execution manifest (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256: 3dfbe1b6...), and analysis artifacts to enable exact replay and to support future confirmatory designs that aim to quantify the operational value of verification and repair in more realistic distributions. Our artifact bundle provides a reproducible template for transparent measurement of verifier marginal impact in NetOps automation evaluations.

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLM families without additional experiments.
Deterministic synthetic task bank and deterministic selection rule — external validity to heterogeneous production change intents and historical failure distributions is limited.

Construct validity depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity to operational regressions; the validator enforces many workflow invariants but does not emulate every stateful control‑plane behavior.
Observed ceiling: baseline success = 1.0 removes the ability to detect verifier marginal benefits under this configuration and power assumptions.
Residual contamination (training data overlap) cannot be entirely excluded despite cryptographic hashing and logging; contamination_summary.csv recorded no flagged items in this run.
